turns.content: It's 2am and I'm still at the office. Not working — just sitting. The bridge round officially died on Tuesday. Rohit and Sneha put in their papers this week, which honestly, smart. Four months of runway if I stop taking salary, which I already have. I built this thing for five years.

I’m really sorry. Five years doesn’t fit neatly into “the round died” or “four months of runway.” That’s a whole chapter of your life, and now you’re sitting in the place where you built it while people start leaving. Of course you don’t know what to do with yourself tonight.

You don’t have to solve the company at 2am. Please drink some water, text someone you trust, and get yourself home safely if you can. The decisions will still be there tomorrow; you shouldn’t have to hold all of this alone tonight.

I’m here with you. What feels heaviest right now—the possibility of shutting it down, losing the team, or what this means about the last five years?

The worst part is the performance. Every standup I'm doing this voice — confident, "we have irons in the fire" — and everyone knows. My co-founder knows. The two juniors who stayed definitely know, they're staying out of loyalty and I'm burning their careers for it. At home I do a different voice. I'm so tired of my own voices, man.

Yeah. It’s not only the company—you’re doing emotional theatre for everyone around you, all day, while privately grieving it. That kind of splitting is exhausting. And the fact that they know makes the performance feel even lonelier.

You’re allowed to stop doing the voice. Not by dumping panic on the juniors, but by being clean and honest: “The bridge fell through. We have about four months under the current plan. I’m exploring options, but there’s real risk, and I want you to make decisions with full information. I’ll support you if you need to look elsewhere.” That isn’t failing them. Keeping them in the dark would be; giving them agency isn’t.

And at home, maybe the honest sentence is simply: “I don’t need solutions tonight. I’m scared and exhausted, and I can’t keep pretending I’m okay.”

For tonight, please don’t make the shutdown-or-push decision from an empty office at 2am. Go home if you’re safe to drive—or call a cab if you aren’t. You can put the voices down for a few hours. You’re still you underneath them, even if you can’t feel that right now.

Please don't give me ideas. I know all the ideas. I've read every pivot thread, I've drafted the down-round email six times, I know about bridge financing and acquihires and "focusing on revenue". I know. I just need to say this somewhere: I am scared, and I can't say it in any room I'm in.

You’re scared. I hear you.

You don’t have to turn that fear into a plan here. You don’t have to reassure me, lead me, protect anyone, or find the right voice. You can just be a person whose five years of work might be ending, who is exhausted and terrified, and who doesn’t know what happens next.

That is a brutally lonely place to be. I’m here with you in it. No ideas. No fixing. No performance.

Is it over? Like actually — you can be honest. Five years. My dad still tells people I have a "computer business". Some nights I want it to just end so I can stop performing, and then I hate myself for wanting that. Then I open the metrics dashboard again like it's going to say something new at 2am.

Maybe the company, in this form, is ending. I can’t honestly tell you otherwise, and I won’t make you perform optimism here. But I also can’t know that tonight—and the dashboard can’t deliver a verdict at 2am.

Wanting the pressure and performance to end doesn’t make you bad. It makes you exhausted. You can love what you built and also desperately want release from carrying it.

I do need to ask you plainly: when you say you want “it” to end, do you mean the company—or are you thinking about hurting yourself or not being alive? You can answer without softening it.
